entry: American membership-only warehouse club chain, headquartered in Issaquah, [[Washington (state)|Washington]]. Its first warehouse opened in [[Seattle]] on September 15, 1983. As of March 2026, it operated 924 warehouses worldwide, 85% of them in North America. As of 2025 it was the third-largest [[Retail|retailer]] in the world, and as of August 2024 the world's largest retailer of beef, poultry, organic produce and wine. Its predecessor, Price Club, had opened in [[San Diego]], [[California]], in 1976.

Distinctive style of dress and/or makeup of an individual or group that reflects class, gender, occupation, ethnicity, nationality, activity or epoch. The word derives from Italian, passed through French, and ultimately from Latin *consuetudo*, meaning custom. It once described typical [[Clothing|clothing]] for activities such as riding or swimming, but its use has narrowed to unusual or out-of-date clothing and attire meant to evoke a change of identity, such as theatrical, [[Halloween]] and [[Mascot|mascot]] costumes. National costume expresses regional identity; in [[Bhutan]], traditional dress is prescribed for men and women, including the monarchy. Stylized theatrical costumes, such as Harlequin and Pantaloon in the [[Commedia dell'arte]], exaggerate a character's traits. Before ready-to-wear apparel, clothing was made by hand, and as late as the early 20th century commercial costumiers were often women who made intimate female dress, millinery and corsetry.

Largest city and seat of government of [[Benin]] (pop., 2012: 679,012). The larger urban area holds over two million people. Cotonou lies on a coastal strip between the [[Atlantic Ocean]] and Lake Nokoué. Its name is said to mean by the river of death in Fon. King Ghezo of Dahomey is thought to have founded it in 1830, and it grew as a center of the slave trade and later of palm oil and [[Cotton|cotton]]. A harbor completed in 1908 spurred rapid growth. The official capital is Porto-Novo, where the national legislature sits, while Cotonou holds most government buildings and foreign embassies. The Autonomous Port of Cotonou is one of the largest in West Africa, and local manufactures include brewing, textiles and cement.

Machine that quickly separates [[Cotton|cotton]] fibers from their seeds, far faster than manual separation. Roller gins were used in the [[Indian subcontinent]] from around the 5th century. The modern mechanical gin was created by American inventor Eli Whitney in 1793 and [[Patent|patented]] in 1794. Whitney's gin used a wire screen and small wire hooks to pull cotton through, while brushes cleared the lint. It made cotton farming more profitable and drove a boom in U.S. production. Because picking then became the bottleneck, it increased the need for laborers, which inadvertently increased the use of enslaved people. Cotton harvesting machines did not arrive until the 1930s. Modern gins can process up to 15 tonnes (33,000 lb) of cotton per hour.

Cushioned [[Furniture|furniture]] for seating several people, also called a sofa, settee or chesterfield. It is usually a bench with upholstered armrests, often fitted with [[Spring (device)|springs]] and tailored cushions and pillows. Although used mainly for seating, a couch may also serve for sleeping, and it is found in homes, [[Hotel|hotels]], offices and waiting rooms. The word comes from [[Middle English]], from Old French *couche*, from a verb meaning to lie down. Couch is most common in [[North America]], Australia and [[South Africa]], while sofa and settee are more common in the [[United Kingdom]] and [[India]]. A loveseat seats two people, and sofa beds, daybeds and futons allow sleeping. The first chesterfield, a deep-buttoned leather sofa, was commissioned by Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield.

Wild cat species (*Puma concolor*) native to the Americas, also called puma, mountain lion, catamount and panther. It is the most widely distributed wild, terrestrial mammal in the Western Hemisphere, ranging from [[Yukon]] in Canada to the southern [[Andes]] in [[Patagonia]]. The cougar is an adaptable, largely solitary ambush predator, and [[Ungulate|ungulates]], particularly [[Deer|deer]], are its primary prey. Intensive hunting after the [[European colonization of the Americas]] and human development caused declines across most of its range. Its eastern population is considered mostly extinct in eastern North America since the early 20th century, except for the isolated Florida panther subpopulation. The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.

Unit of [[Electric charge|electric charge]] in the [[International System of Units]] (SI), symbol C. It is the charge delivered by a current of one [[Ampere|ampere]] flowing for one [[Second|second]]. Since the 2019 redefinition of SI base units fixed the elementary charge, one coulomb equals approximately 6.241509×10¹⁸ elementary charges. Every [[Farad|farad]] of capacitance can hold one coulomb per volt, and one ampere-hour equals 3600 C. Static electricity from rubbing materials typically involves a few microcoulombs, while a [[Lightning|lightning]] bolt typically carries around 15 C, and up to 350 C for large bolts. The unit is named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, and the International Electrical Congress approved it as the unit of electric charge in 1881.

Law of physics describing the electrostatic force between two electrically charged particles at rest. The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, along the line joining them. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb published the law in 1785, though earlier investigators including [[Daniel Bernoulli]] and [[Alessandro Volta]] had suspected an inverse-square dependence. Like [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newton's law of universal gravitation]], it is an inverse-square law, but electrostatic forces can attract or repel, while gravity always attracts. The law was essential to the development of [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]] and has been tested from 10⁻¹⁶ m to 10⁸ m.

International organization, founded in 1949, to uphold [[Human rights|human rights]], [[Democracy|democracy]] and the [[Rule of law|rule of law]] in Europe. It is Europe's oldest intergovernmental organization, with 46 member states, and is headquartered in [[Strasbourg]], [[France]]. Unlike the [[European Union]], it cannot make binding laws, but it has produced international standards and treaties, including the European Convention on Human Rights (1950). The European Court of Human Rights rules on alleged violations of the convention, and its judgments are legally binding on the state concerned. [[Russia]] became the first country expelled from the council, following its 2022 invasion of [[Ukraine]]. The organization's annual ordinary budget is 656 million euros.

Fictional vampire and title antagonist of [[Bram Stoker]]'s gothic horror novel *Dracula* (1897). He is considered the archetypal vampire of later fiction, known for turning victims into vampires by biting them. Some traits may derive from the 15th-century Wallachian prince [[Vlad the Impaler|Vlad III Dracula]], a link proposed only decades after publication. It is widely believed that the character was inspired by Sir Henry Irving, for whom Stoker was personal assistant. He is one of the best-known fictional figures of the [[Victorian era]].

Period of Catholic revival, also called the Catholic Reformation, that responded to the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. It is often dated from the Council of Trent (1545–1563) to the end of the European wars of religion in 1648, though this periodization is controversial. Its efforts included apologetic writings, reform of religious orders, seminaries to train priests, and new devotional movements focused on a personal relationship with Christ. The [[Ignatius of Loyola|Society of Jesus]] was founded in 1540 as an order devoted to education, obedience to the [[Pope|pope]] and missionary work. The Roman [[Inquisition]] was reorganized in 1542. The term is a translation of German *Gegenreformation*, coined by late 18th-century German historians as a negative label for Catholic repression and popularized by [[Leopold von Ranke]]. Catholic historians tended to avoid it, and Protestant historians often preferred to speak of Catholic reform.

Military and political actions aimed at defeating irregular forces, which can be considered war by a state against a non-state adversary. Insurgency and counterinsurgency have been waged since ancient history, and modern thinking developed during decolonization. Counterinsurgency combines conventional military operations with [[Propaganda|propaganda]], psychological operations and [[Assassination|assassinations]], as well as political, economic and civic measures. It may seek to win the hearts and minds of a population supporting an [[Insurgency|insurgency]], or it may use indiscriminate violence against civilians suspected of loyalty to insurgents. French campaigns in [[Algeria]] and Indochina shaped later doctrine. Analysts disagree on whether population-centric approaches that address grievances or enemy-centric, coercive methods are more effective.

Relationship of two or more simultaneous melodic lines, called voices, that are [[Harmony|harmonically]] dependent on each other yet independent in rhythm and melodic contour. The term comes from Latin *punctus contra punctum*, meaning point against point, or note against note. It developed most strongly in the European classical tradition, especially during the Renaissance and the Baroque period, and is taught in Western pedagogy through a system of species. Imitative counterpoint repeats a melodic idea across voices, as in the [[Fugue|fugue]], the most complex contrapuntal convention. Free counterpoint often uses non-traditional harmonies, chromaticism and dissonance. [[Johann Sebastian Bach]] is regarded as one of the greatest masters of counterpoint, and his three-part invention in F minor combines three independent melodies.

Subdivisions of [[England]] with three legal definitions: 48 ceremonial counties used for lieutenancy, 84 metropolitan and non-metropolitan counties, and 39 historic counties. The historic counties, mostly formed as shires of earlier kingdoms, were used for justice, constituencies and the militia. Administrative counties with elected councils were created in 1889. Since 1974 the local government counties have covered England except [[Greater London]] and the [[Isles of Scilly]], and the historic counties have not been used for local government. Counties are also used for culture, tourism and sport.

Historic administrative divisions of the [[Ireland|island of Ireland]], traditionally numbering 32. They began as Norman structures and developed as the powers of barons and nobility waned. Six of the traditional counties became part of [[Northern Ireland]] in 1921, where counties ceased to be used for local government in 1973. The [[Republic of Ireland]] has 26 counties, 3 cities and 2 cities and counties for local government, after some counties were split. The word usually precedes the name, as in County Roscommon.

Music genre originating in the United States, known for ballads and dance tunes with traditional lyrics and harmonies. Also called country and western, it was once known as hillbilly music, and the term was popularized in the 1940s. It developed in the South from [[Folk music|British folk music]] brought by immigrants, [[Appalachian Mountains|Appalachian]] music, cowboy ballads, African American folk songs and spirituals. Typical instruments include banjos, [[Mandolin|mandolins]], fiddles, [[Harmonica|harmonicas]] and [[Guitar|guitars]]. Radio broadened its audience in the 1920s; the Grand Ole Opry began airing in 1925 from [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. The U.S. Congress has recognized Bristol, Tennessee, as the "Birthplace of Country Music," based on 1927 recording sessions. In 2023, 45% of Americans reported listening to country music.

Administrative subdivision of most [[United States|U.S.]] states, typically with defined boundaries and some level of governmental authority. The term is used in 47 states; [[Louisiana]] uses parishes, [[Alaska]] uses boroughs, and [[Connecticut]] uses councils of governments or planning regions as county equivalents. County powers vary by state. In Hawaii, counties provide almost all services, while in Rhode Island they have no government power. As of 2022 there were 3,144 counties and county equivalents in the 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Illegal and overt attempt by a [[Military organization|military organization]] or other government elite to unseat an incumbent leader or government. From French, literally meaning stroke of state. A self-coup occurs when a leader who came to power legally tries to stay in power illegally. By one estimate there were 457 coup attempts from 1950 to 2010, half of them successful, with most occurring in the mid-1960s. Coups since the [[Cold War]] have been more likely to produce democratic systems than Cold War coups, though coups still mostly perpetuate [[Authoritarianism|authoritarianism]]. Failed coups in authoritarian systems tend to strengthen the ruler. A putsch is a minority reactionary coup, a term first used for the Züriputsch of 1839 in Switzerland. A soft coup overthrows a government without force.

Choice and willingness to confront [[Pain|pain]], danger, uncertainty or intimidation, also called bravery or valor. Physical courage is bravery in the face of pain, hardship or death, while moral courage is the ability to act rightly despite popular opposition, shame or personal loss. The classical [[Virtue|virtue]] of fortitude, also translated as courage, includes perseverance and patience. Philosophers including [[Socrates]], [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] wrote on courage, and the Chinese text [[Tao Te Ching]] addresses both physical and moral courage. Professor Daniel Putman argues that courage involves deliberate choice in the face of fearful circumstances for the sake of a worthy goal, and that the balance of fear and confidence determines whether courage is distorted.

Person or organization that delivers a message, package or letter from one place or person to another, usually on a commercial contract basis. Couriers differ from ordinary mail through speed, security, tracking and signature. Large companies, including DHL, FedEx and UPS, operate hub-and-spoke networks. In antiquity, messages were carried by runners, homing pigeons and horseback riders. The [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] courier Pheidippides is said to have run 26 miles from [[Marathon]] to [[Athens]] in 490 BC, and the race known as the marathon is named for this run.

Institution, often governmental, with authority to adjudicate legal disputes and administer justice in civil, criminal and administrative matters under the [[Rule of law|rule of law]]. Courts usually consist of [[Judge|judges]] or other judicial officers and are established by legislation or a constitution. A court's jurisdiction is its power to decide certain kinds of questions or petitions. Types include [[Trial|trial]] courts, appellate courts, administrative courts, international courts and tribunals. The system of courts is known as the [[Judiciary|judiciary]]. The word derives from French *cour*, an enclosed yard where a sovereign and his entourage met to settle disputes. According to [[William Blackstone]]'s *Commentaries on the Laws of England*, a civil court requires at least three parties: the plaintiff, the defendant and the judge.

American actress, director and producer. She rose to international prominence as Monica Geller in the [[NBC]] sitcom *Friends* (1994–2004) and as Gale Weathers in the *Scream* horror film franchise, beginning with the first film in 1996. Her later series include *Cougar Town* (2009–2015). Cox has also directed films, including *Just Before I Go* (2014), and holds a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Period when some couples become familiar with each other before a possible marriage or committed relationship. It may begin after a betrothal and end with a wedding, and may be private, public or a formal arrangement with family approval. Traditionally, a man was expected to court a woman, encouraging her to accept a proposal. As a social practice, courtship is relatively recent, emerging within the last few centuries. In most past societies, marriages were arranged by parents for economic stability and political alliances. From about 1700 a movement toward individual emancipation spread, and women gradually won voting rights, beginning with [[Norway]] in 1913. In many Western countries courtship became increasingly self-initiated, though many countries still practice [[Arranged marriage|arranged marriages]]. Anthropologists and sociologists link courtship with [[Marriage|marriage]] and the [[Family|family]], institutions that have changed with technology and medicine. In non-human animals, courtship refers to sexual behavior that precedes copulation.

Traditional North African dish of small granules of rolled semolina, steamed and often served with a stew. It is a staple of the [[Maghreb|Maghrebi]] cuisines of [[Algeria]], [[Tunisia]], [[Mauritania]], [[Morocco]] and [[Libya]]. It entered French and European cuisine in the early 20th century through the [[French colonial empire]]. [[UNESCO]] added couscous to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020. The word is probably of Berber origin, first recorded in early 17th-century French from Arabic *kuskus*.

Relative who is the child of one's parent's [[Sibling|sibling]], also called a first cousin. In the English [[Kinship|kinship]] system, cousins share a common ancestor but are at least two generations removed from it. The degree measures how distant the relationship is from the common ancestor, starting with one for first cousins, while removal measures the difference in generations between cousins. A first cousin once removed is the child of one's first cousin or the first cousin of one's parent. First cousins share on average 12.5% of their genetic material. Children of first-cousin unions face a risk of autosomal recessive disorders rising to 6–7%, roughly double the baseline of 3–4%. The term kissing cousin is used for a distant relative familiar enough to be greeted with a [[Kiss|kiss]].
